text:
Happy belated Veterans Day — and a deep, heartfelt 🙏 Thank you!!!!!
I just watched this short but extraordinary interview with Lieutenant Brad Snyder on NBC10 Philadelphia’s Philly Live, and it stayed with me. What a beautiful man. What a beautiful human being. The kind of person who makes you stop, feel a little smaller in the best way, and feel genuinely honored that people like him walk this earth while we are here to share it with them.
Snyder is a Navy veteran, Naval Academy graduate, former Explosive Ordnance Disposal officer who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, and an eight-time Paralympic medalist (six gold, two silver). On September 7, 2011, while embedded with special operations forces in Afghanistan and helping wounded partners, he was blinded by a massive IED. Exactly one year later, to the day, he stood on the London Paralympic podium as a gold medalist. He later added more swimming medals in Rio, transitioned to paratriathlon, and won gold again in Tokyo. He has written a book about the journey, speaks on leadership and adversity, and continues to serve in new ways — including, on this night, as honorary captain for the 76ers’ military appreciation night.
In the interview he doesn’t dwell on the injury or the medals. He talks about how the military taught him to treat every new challenge — bomb school, jump training, sudden blindness, learning to swim or do triathlon without sight — as simply the next thing to master. He talks about the harder work of rebuilding confidence once the uniform comes off, realizing that what remains is character, the ability to lead people toward shared purpose, and the capacity to keep giving. Sports, he says, gave him validation that he still had something left to offer his community and his country. And that is what drives him now: sharing the story so others can tackle hard things and navigate adversity with grace.
What moved me most was his simple, clear view of Veterans Day. He is proud of the special night with the Sixers and Team Toyota, but he points out that every single moment, tens of thousands of service members are deployed somewhere in the world — away from their families, sleep-deprived, not eating well — preserving the ordinary freedoms and security the rest of us get to take for granted. Taking even a moment to be grateful for them, he says, is magical. His advice to anyone struggling to find purpose is equally quiet and powerful: make the most of every interaction. We all have the ability to empower, love, and inspire one another in the ordinary moments of a day.
He loves the Sixers. He’s here, in the area, with his family nearby, serving as honorary captain for their military appreciation night. There is something especially warm and local about that — a man of his caliber choosing to show up, smile, say “Go Sixers,” and use the platform to shine a light on those still serving. It feels personal. It feels like ours.
I cherish people like Lieutenant Brad Snyder. In a world that can feel noisy, cynical, and quick to depreciate sacrifice, he is living proof of steadiness, humility, and continued service. He took one of the hardest possible turns life can hand someone and kept moving forward with purpose, without self-pity, and with a genuine desire to lift others. Watching him speak — calm, grateful, focused on the people still out there and on the simple act of bringing out the best in one another — is a reminder of the best of what we are capable of.
To Lieutenant Snyder: thank you for your service, for your example, and for the way you carry yourself. To every veteran, every active-duty service member, and every military family: thank you. The life so many of us get to live is possible because of people like you. We are honored to share the earth with you while we are here.
Go Sixers. And thank you.

text:
Recenty interview of $RKLB CEO @Peter_J_Beck with @FunOfInvesting 

Q1. Was there anything in Rocket Lab's latest earnings report or earnings call that you felt didn't receive enough attention from retail investors or institutional investors?

Peter Beck:

I think people pretty much understood the results. Selling $1 billion worth of launches in a quarter is a significant achievement.

One slide we're particularly proud of shows our continued execution and growth year after year. It's one thing to have a strong growth year followed by a flat year and then another strong year. What's impressive is seeing consistent growth year after year.

We're approaching nearly $1 billion in revenue this year, and I think the entire team is very proud of that achievement.

Q2. Neutron was originally targeted for 2024 and is now expected in 2027. What have you learned throughout the development process, and what gives you confidence in the revised timeline?

Peter Beck:

I've learned that I'm not particularly good at estimating timelines for medium-class launch vehicles.

In all seriousness, Rocket Lab operates with an optimistic approach to scheduling. We use what's called a green-light schedule, which assumes everything goes well, with no development issues along the way. That represents the earliest possible delivery timeline.

The philosophy is that if you build too much buffer into a schedule, you inevitably consume it. By not building in excessive buffer, you give yourself the best opportunity to deliver on time.

We've encountered challenges along the way, particularly because we're developing technologies that nobody has done before. Rocket development is difficult, and delays are part of the process. However, I think our timeline is relatively normal compared with the history of rocket development.

I'd much rather discover an issue with a rocket tank during ground testing than discover it during flight.

Our development philosophy is also different. We're not simply trying to get the first rocket onto the launch pad. We want the second, third, fourth, and fifth rockets to follow quickly. We've been investing in the processes and infrastructure needed to make that possible.

Q3. What is Rocket Lab doing today to prepare for scaling Neutron beyond its first flight? What are the biggest challenges in transitioning from the first launch to a regular launch business?

Peter Beck:

One way to evaluate the seriousness of a rocket program is to look at its investment in recovery barges.

A barge is far more complicated than a floating piece of steel. It requires megawatts of power generation, thrusters, autonomous capabilities, and the ability to maintain its position within sub-meter accuracy in the Atlantic Ocean.

Building a barge is a two-to-three-year investment, so getting started early is extremely important.

We've also invested heavily in factories and manufacturing infrastructure. For example, our engine factory can now produce an engine in a matter of days.

Another important part of our strategy is how we approach manufacturing. Traditionally, we would build one component, test it, confirm that it works, and then build the second one.

However, that serial approach takes time.

For components we're highly confident won't change, we've already built multiple units. For components with more uncertainty, we're still building more than one, but we're taking a measured approach because some of those components could ultimately be scrapped.

This is the fastest way to scale production and prepare for a regular launch cadence.

Q4. How many annual Neutron launches would Rocket Lab need to become profitable?

Peter Beck:

The economics turn positive relatively quickly, particularly at a launch price of $70 million.

We expect to cover the costs of the overall operation at a relatively low launch cadence, well below 10 launches per year.

Our target gross margin model for Neutron is similar to Electron: approximately 50%.

Two factors primarily influence launch profitability:

Launch cadence: Higher launch frequency allows us to spread fixed costs across more launches, including facilities and launch infrastructure. This is particularly important for Electron because it isn't reusable.

Reusability: Neutron benefits from reusability, which allows us to amortize infrastructure and operational costs more quickly.

As launch cadence increases, the economics become increasingly attractive.

Q5. Neutron's $70 million launch price surprised some investors. Is this driven by supply-demand dynamics, or is there an upper limit to what customers are willing to pay?

Peter Beck:

It's a combination of factors.

Launch capacity is scarce, and we have a limited number of available slots. That makes those slots extremely valuable.

From the beginning of the Neutron program, I said we would sell our first launches when we could command full price.

Naturally, customers expect discounts for rockets that haven't flown yet, particularly during the early stages of development when there's no physical hardware available to inspect.

However, everything has worked out as we expected. We wanted to enter a market where demand for launch services was already very strong, and we had no intention of discounting Neutron.

Not a single Neutron launch has been discounted. In fact, we've seen the opposite.

When customers evaluate launch vehicles currently in development, only two companies have successfully demonstrated the ability to take a rocket from a clean-sheet design to a high-cadence launch vehicle. Rocket Lab is one of them.

When customers visit us, see our hardware, and understand our track record, they have confidence that we can deliver.

Q6. Rocket Lab's acquisition of Iridium is expected to close in mid-2027. What are the biggest integration challenges, and how long will it take for operational synergies to translate into financial results?

Peter Beck:

Some synergies will translate immediately. For example, there are straightforward opportunities to eliminate duplicated corporate functions between two public companies.

The bigger challenge is that Iridium is a relatively large acquisition. Its employee headcount is approximately twice that of the largest company we've previously acquired and integrated, which was SolAero.

However, SolAero and Iridium share similarities. Both are traditional space companies with long operating histories.

I think we did an excellent job integrating SolAero, and I expect the same with Iridium.

The more interesting challenge is that Rocket Lab is primarily made up of rocket and satellite engineers, whereas Iridium is a services company.

One of the reasons we decided to acquire rather than build this capability ourselves is Iridium's tremendous customer base and expertise in operating space-based services businesses.

We'll work alongside their team and learn from their experience.

Longer term, the opportunity is significant. When you own your own rocket, build your own satellites, and operate services from space, you create a powerful business model.

Combining the two companies will allow us to bring new services and programs to market that Iridium could not have pursued independently.

Q7. Looking three to five years ahead, how meaningful could the operational synergies become?

Peter Beck:

I certainly hope it doesn't take three to five years. That's an extraordinarily long timeframe for Rocket Lab. I measure this in months, not years.

Both teams have already identified numerous exciting services and opportunities that we can pursue as a combined company.

I also want to emphasize that our ambition isn't simply to become the world's leading safety-critical communications company.

Communications will be one important part of our services business, but you should expect Rocket Lab to offer multiple services in the future.

Q8. Rocket Lab has discussed potentially dedicating half of Neutron's launch capacity to its own satellite services. How do you balance near-term revenue from external launches against the opportunity to generate larger recurring revenue streams from operating your own satellites?

Peter Beck:

We approach this very carefully because there is still a significant shortage of launch capacity in the industry.

We need to continue providing launch services to the broader space community. Given the size of our Space Systems business, limited launch availability would also negatively affect national security and commercial programs.

We will always ensure that a steady supply of launch capacity remains available to the industry.

At the same time, we need to preserve enough capacity to pursue our own opportunities.

There is an important economic distinction here. Launching someone else's satellite generates a one-time revenue opportunity. Launching our own satellite can create recurring revenue for the next 10 years.

The economics of launching your own infrastructure are significantly stronger over the long term.

However, we must balance that opportunity against our responsibility to support the broader space industry, which also affects other parts of our business.

Q9. Rocket Lab has signed StarCloud as a Neutron customer, but you've expressed skepticism about the economics of large-scale orbital data centers. Is this a market Rocket Lab intends to pursue as a meaningful future revenue opportunity?

Peter Beck:

Sometimes it's great to be a pioneer, and sometimes it's better to stay slightly behind the front line and observe how things develop.

I've been proven wrong on multiple occasions, so I wouldn't take my comments about this market as gospel.

I'm an engineer first and probably an entrepreneur second. Naturally, I approach new technologies with a healthy degree of skepticism.

We're certainly participating in the market, and if orbital data centers turn out to be a significant opportunity, I think Rocket Lab is in an excellent position to execute.

However, for now, I'd rather be a fast follower than lead the market.

Q10. So, if orbital data centers become a major market, Rocket Lab will participate, but it's not an immediate strategic priority?

Peter Beck:

I'm certainly not going to bet the business on it.

We're happy to support other companies, as we've already demonstrated. We're watching the market closely and will contribute where appropriate.

If it becomes a genuinely significant opportunity, we'll pursue it.

Q11. As government satellite programs approach completion, how much future growth do you expect from repeat orders and constellation replacements versus winning entirely new contracts?

Peter Beck:

One attractive aspect of defense contracts is that many of these programs have bipartisan support. They involve capabilities that the country desperately needs.

As a result, they're relatively resilient to changes in political administrations.

These platforms have defined operational lifetimes and eventually need to be replaced.

Additionally, as threats evolve, countermeasures and defense capabilities must evolve as well.

The defense industry is never static. As adversaries develop new technologies, new capabilities and countermeasures become necessary.

Unlike some commercial satellite applications, where infrastructure can remain unchanged for a long time, defense systems require continuous development and modernization.

I therefore expect a relatively consistent stream of opportunities and contracts in this market.

Q12. Following the midterm elections, do you anticipate increased congressional scrutiny or efforts to diversify government contractors, potentially creating new opportunities for Rocket Lab?

Peter Beck:

I think the environment will remain relatively agnostic.

There is strong bipartisan support for many space-based defense missions, and I don't believe anyone will eliminate programs that are critically important to national security.

Historically, these programs have remained relatively consistent despite changes in government.

Q13. Do you expect defense and national security to become a larger part of the global space industry?

Peter Beck:

Yes, but perhaps in a different way.

Unfortunately, we're living in increasingly fragile geopolitical times.

One of the most common things we hear from our friends and allies outside the United States is that they want sovereign space capabilities.

This is particularly true in Europe.

That's one of the reasons we established Rocket Lab Europe and made the Mynaric acquisition. We're working to establish a strong foothold in Europe because we see it as a major future market, particularly for defense and national security applications.

Q14. What is the biggest misconception investors have about Rocket Lab today?

Peter Beck:

I think the misconception is actually in the company's name.

Everyone assumes Rocket Lab is primarily about rockets. In some respects, that's understandable because without rockets, you can't do much in space.

Launch is an extremely difficult business, but having access to space gives you the ability to do so much more.

A significant portion of our business has nothing to do with rockets. We have a substantial Space Systems business, and soon we'll have an even larger presence in space services.

Perhaps I should have called the company Space Lab instead of Rocket Lab!

Q15. How large do you see the services business becoming, particularly following the Iridium acquisition?

Peter Beck:

Services will eventually dwarf everything else by a significant margin.

If you look at the total addressable markets:

Launch: Approximately $10 billion.
Space Systems: Approximately $30 billion.
Space Services: Approximately $320 billion.

Depending on which industry estimates you look at, the space services market could exceed $1 trillion by 2035.

Space services have always represented the largest opportunity. After all, providing services is ultimately the reason we go to space.

Q16. Rocket Lab has developed a very passionate retail investor following. Is there anything you believe the market misunderstands about the company, or any message you'd like to share with retail shareholders?

Peter Beck:

First, I'd like to thank everyone for their support and belief in the company. We genuinely appreciate it and take that responsibility very seriously.

There's nothing more rewarding than hearing stories from shareholders who invested at $3.80, maintained their conviction in the company, and have done well enough to achieve meaningful milestones, such as buying a house.

Those stories are fantastic.

We take our responsibility to shareholders extremely seriously.

At the end of the day, our job is to create shareholder value.

Space is exciting, and what we're building is incredible, but the company must ultimately become profitable, financially robust, and sustainable over the long term.

That is our number one priority: creating value for shareholders.

text:
Vlad, I think you’ve fundamentally mischaracterized AST SpaceMobile’s strategic position. You’ve taken one legitimate industry constraint and constructed an entirely backward narrative around it.

$ASTS isn’t being forced into building rockets because it has nowhere else to turn. It has already secured launch agreements covering more than 100 BlueBird satellites through 2028, involving SpaceX, Blue Origin and others. Blue Origin publicly advertises its multiyear relationship with AST SpaceMobile. Those relationships aren’t disappearing when Blacklift arrives.

Blacklift is additive, not a rescue operation.

Consider the actual strategic trajectory. AST has developed proprietary satellite technology, demonstrated direct-to-device broadband capabilities, established relationships with major mobile network operators, expanded into sovereign and government markets, and is now vertically integrating launch.

That isn’t a company running out of options. It’s a company accumulating them.

And the implications extend far beyond launch availability.

Blacklift offers control over deployment cadence, mission-specific vehicle optimization, launch flexibility, and potentially dramatically lower marginal costs as flight rates scale. AST has even acquired perpetual manufacturing rights to the engines. This is industrial integration across an increasingly differentiated technology platform.

Meanwhile, AST’s addressable market is expanding beyond conventional cellular broadband into sovereign infrastructure, defense, AI-enabled services, radar, sensing and other space-based capabilities. The implications for orbital infrastructure demand are enormous.

You correctly identify launch scarcity as an industry constraint. But you’ve overlooked the much bigger opportunity: AST can continue purchasing launch services while developing the ability to internalize their economics.

And importantly, this is not some clean-sheet engine development fantasy. AST is leveraging existing Miranda and Vira engine architecture and Firefly’s engineering capabilities. The 2028 target is ambitious, certainly, but ambition and desperation are not synonyms.

The possibility of a multi-trillion-dollar enterprise remains speculative. But if AST ultimately achieves that scale, this kind of vertical integration could become one of the defining strategic decisions that made it possible.

You’re looking at Blacklift as evidence of AST’s disadvantage.

I’d suggest you’re witnessing the opposite: a company with an unusually differentiated technology platform building the industrial infrastructure to capture an opportunity far larger than its original business model.

This isn’t AST playing the only hand it holds. It’s AST expanding the number of hands it can play, while retaining the ones it already has.

An AI-native company should be designed around 5 principles:

1. Own the context: 
Biz data, relationships, rules, and history are accessible through a coherent system.

2. Automate the operations: 
Agents and deterministic workflows perform as much routine work as reliably possible.

3. Buy the primitives: 
Use established infra and specialized services where building offers little advantage.

4. Generate the experiences: 
Create human interfaces when and where they deliver value.

5. Govern the autonomy: 
Humans establish objectives, constraints, approval boundaries, and accountability.

text:
I'm not afraid of a family leaving Martin County schools.

I'm afraid of us giving them a reason to.
That's the difference between a district that fights school choice and one that competes in it.

Some will spend their energy complaining about charters, scholarships, and private schools.

Blaming the law. Blaming the funding. Blaming everyone but themselves.

I'd rather spend mine making sure no family ever wants to leave.

When a family walks away, they're telling us something. Maybe we didn't listen. Maybe we didn't offer what their child needed. Maybe we got comfortable.

Competition exposes that. And that's exactly why I welcome it.

Florida trusted parents with the power to choose. I trust them too. If they choose someone else, that's our report card. If they choose us, we earned it.

No protection. No guarantees. No excuses.

Just a promise: in Martin County, we will work every single day to be your first choice.

That's the Martin Standard.

In light of the latest rendezvous involving Trump’s envoys and their “peace proposals,” let me try to explain to my dear Europeans what’s really going on.

Here we go.

Putin has realized that as long as the EU continues supporting Ukraine, he cannot defeat it on the battlefield.

Of course, he still has another option: destroying Ukraine’s infrastructure this winter in an attempt to break the Ukrainian people’s will. But the Kremlin leader doesn’t have much faith in that plan either.

So he needs to force Europe to abandon its support for Ukraine at any cost.

Russia’s hybrid attacks against Europe are producing some results, but progress is so slow that Putin might run out of time before achieving his goal.

He sees a much more effective option: launching long-range strikes against European countries, starting with the Baltic states, to intimidate Europeans once and for all.

That’s why, with Witkoff and Kushner’s help, he’s staging a performance called “We Warned You!”

The goal is to gradually condition everyone to accept the Kremlin’s grievances against Europe as legitimate, while simultaneously giving the United States an excuse to abandon its European allies:
“We offered you a deal, but you wouldn’t listen.”

So, dear Europeans, unless you wake up right now and realize that the only way forward is to destroy Russia’s economic capacity to wage wars of aggression, war will reach your doorstep sooner than anyone thinks. Unfortunately.
